(see Mary Jnl i 390–91, 395–6). Trelawny himself later recalled that S. never walked out
with his wife during his time in their company (The Diary of W. M. Rossetti 1870–1873, ed.
 Odette Bornand (1977) 170). Certainly, Mary was often distant and unresponsive to S. in
their final months together, and also sometimes bad-tempered, although there was much
in her life at that time to explain a depression, with constant harassment from her father,
her illnesses and dangerously failed pregnancy, and the constant dark shadow of the deaths
of two young children. S., on the other hand, enjoyed generally better health than usual,
and at times a more settled serenity, in the winter months of 1822, and clearly found his
feelings for Jane Williams deepening. He wrote to John Gisborne on 12 January 1822 ‘The
Williams’s are well. Mrs. W., more amiable and beautiful than ever, and a sort of spirit of
embodied peace in our circle of tempests. So much for first impressions!’ (L ii 376).
